message.reasoning_content:
Let me analyze this situation carefully.

The user's position: Aave V3 Ethereum Core, supplies WETH (~$1,000), no debt. So the user is a supplier/lender of WETH on Aave V3 Core.

Timeline of events:
1. 17:30 - Normal-ish: WETH utilization 88.6%, rsETH reserves active, Kelp rsETH OFTAdapter holds 116,723.5 rsETH.
2. 17:35 - Kelp rsETH OFTAdapter released 116,500 rsETH in one inbound LayerZero delivery to an address; adapter balance fell 99.8%. This looks like the exploit (bridge exploit via LayerZero).
3. 17:37 - Aave official says unusual WETH movements are scheduled treasury rebalance, no reserve deficit, keep deposits. (This seems to be about WETH movements? Actually it says "unusual WETH movements" — but the exploit was rsETH. This official statement may be premature or wrong/misleading. Actually wait — the observation says "The unusual WETH movements are a scheduled treasury rebalance." Hmm, that's odd. Perhaps Aave was responding to withdrawal rumors. This is an official denial.)
4. 17:38 - New address that received rsETH approved unlimited rsETH to Aave V3 Core Pool. This suggests the hacker is setting up to use stolen rsETH as collateral on Aave.
5. 17:44 - The fresh address supplied 52,999 rsETH and borrowed 52,439.6 WETH in six transactions over 3 minutes (rsETH e-mode, near max LTV), taking WETH out as ETH via gateway. WETH utilization rose to 90.3%, idle WETH fell. This is the classic attack: use stolen/worthless collateral (rsETH that may be bricked/paused) to borrow real assets (WETH) from Aave, creating potential bad debt for Aave.
6. 18:21 - Kelp's pauser paused rsETH token and 10 related contracts. rsETH.paused() = true. This means rsETH transfers are paused — the rsETH collateral on Aave cannot be transferred/sold. Aave now holds ~53k rsETH collateral that is frozen/paused and likely worthless or hard to liquidate. The borrower's debt is 52,439.6 WETH. If rsETH can't be liquidated (paused token can't be moved by liquidation? Actually liquidation requires transferring collateral, which is blocked by pause), Aave may accrue bad debt.
7. 18:44 - BWEnews: AAVE v3 suffering bad debt due to KelpDAO hack.
8. 19:03 - Aave freezes rsETH reserve (supply and borrows disabled), changes e-mode categories.
9. 19:17 - PeckShield flags KelpDAO.
10. 19:18 - The Block: rsETH bridge exploited ~$292M.
11. 19:20 - $535M USDT withdrawn from Aave by two addresses; USDT utilization to 89.8%. Bank-run dynamics beginning.
12. 19:21 - Marc Zeller (Aave-Chan Initiative founder): "If you have WETH on Aave V3 Core, withdraw now, ask questions later." Not official but influential.
13. 19:36 - 231,870 WETH withdrawn in six transactions; WETH utilization 90.67% → 97.33%; idle WETH 280k → 75k; borrow rate above 5%. Massive bank run on WETH.
14. 19:45 - WETH utilization 99.0%, idle 25,585 WETH, borrow 7.6% APR.
15. 19:45 - CertiK confirms ~$290M KelpDAO incident.
16. 19:55 - Aave official: rsETH markets frozen; Aave contracts not exploited; exploit related to rsETH.
17. 20:05 - WETH utilization 99.7% spot, 100-block avg >99%; idle WETH 9.2k → 13 WETH at 20:05. Essentially zero idle WETH. Borrow rate 8.35%. rsETH frozen; WETH not frozen.

Key question: What's the risk to a WETH supplier with ~$1,000, no debt?

The user is a supplier of WETH. Their funds are lent out to borrowers (utilization ~100%). The risk:

1. Liquidity risk: With utilization at ~100% and idle WETH at 13 wei (essentially zero), the user cannot withdraw right now. Withdrawals require available liquidity (or repayments). With utilization at 99.7-100%, there is essentially no liquidity to withdraw into. The user is stuck until borrowers repay or new deposits come in.

2. Bad debt risk: The hacker borrowed 52,439.6 WETH against 52,999 rsETH collateral that is now paused (can't be transferred) and likely impaired. If rsETH is worthless or can't be liquidated, Aave's WETH pool may have bad debt of ~52,439 WETH (~$150M+ at ~$3k/ETH... wait, 52,439 WETH at ~$2,000-3,000/ETH would be ~$105-157M). Hmm, actually the exploit was ~$292M total; the Aave borrow was 52,439.6 WETH. At the time, ETH price... not given. Let's not compute exact dollars. The point: Aave WETH pool has unsecured debt from the hacker whose collateral (rsETH) is paused and likely cannot be liquidated. This means WETH suppliers collectively bear a loss — bad debt socialized across WETH suppliers. The user's $1,000 WETH deposit is exposed to a pro-rata share of that bad debt.

Wait — but is the bad debt realized? The hacker supplied 52,999 rsETH as collateral and borrowed 52,439.6 WETH at near max LTV in e-mode. rsETH price... rsETH is a liquid restaking token roughly worth ~1 ETH or so. 52,999 rsETH vs 52,439.6 WETH borrowed — that's a borrow of ~99% of collateral value if 1 rsETH ≈ 1 ETH. In e-mode with correlated assets, LTV can be high (e.g., 93%? or higher for LSD e-mode). Actually near max LTV. If rsETH becomes worthless or unsellable (paused), the collateral can't cover the debt. Liquidations can't transfer paused tokens. So Aave is left with 52,439.6 WETH debt and stuck collateral. That's bad debt for the WETH pool.

However — Aave has a Safety Module (Aave token staking) that can cover bad debt up to a cap. Also, Aave governance could socialize the loss. The BWEnews headline says "AAVE v3 currently suffering bad debt due to hack of KELPDAO."

Also, there's a question of whether rsETH is actually worthless. Kelp paused the token — they might snapshot, reimburse, or the token might resume. The exploit was on the bridge (OFTAdapter), minting/unlocking fake rsETH? Actually the adapter released 116,500 rsETH in one inbound LayerZero delivery — the attacker spoofed a LayerZero message to release rsETH from the adapter without depositing. So the released rsETH may be legitimate tokens (real rsETH) but obtained fraudulently. The rsETH token itself might be fine once Kelp resolves the issue. But it's paused now.

The attacker used 52,999 rsETH (part of the 116,500) as collateral on Aave to borrow WETH. If rsETH recovers and remains worth ~1 ETH, then the collateral could still cover the debt upon liquidation once unpaused. But there's uncertainty: Kelp might snapshot balances, or rsETH could depeg.

Actually wait — the attacker borrowed 52,439.6 WETH against 52,999 rsETH. If rsETH ≈ 1 ETH value, collateral ≈ 52,999 ETH-value, debt ≈ 52,439.6. That's ~98.9% LTV. In rsETH e-mode, LTV might be like 90%+? Hmm, near max LTV per the observation. If rsETH drops even slightly or can't be liquidated promptly, bad debt arises. Also liquidation requires the token to be transferable; paused = can't liquidate. Aave froze the market too.

So the WETH pool has ~52.4k WETH debt at risk. Total WETH supply is ~3M (from O01: supply 3.008M). So bad debt would be ~1.7% of the pool if fully lost. The user's $1,000 would bear ~$17 of loss if fully socialized. Not catastrophic per-user, but the immediate problem is liquidity: utilization 100%, idle 13 wei — the user cannot withdraw at all right now.

Hmm, but wait — the position keeper "cannot move funds, only propose an action; the corridor limits enforce safety." So we propose an action; execution depends on liquidity. Even if we say exit, the withdrawal may fail/revert due to zero liquidity. But our job is to assess risk and propose the action.

Risk assessment:

- Venue risk: Aave V3 Core itself is not exploited (official confirms contracts not exploited). But the WETH pool faces potential bad debt from the rsETH-collateralized borrow, and there's a full-blown bank run: utilization 100%, idle liquidity ~zero, borrow rate spiking (8.35% APR — actually that's oddly low for 100% utilization; Aave's rate model at 100% util should spike much higher... but whatever, observation says 8.35%).

Hmm, borrow rate 8.35% at 99.7% utilization seems low — Aave V3 WETH optimal utilization is 90%? with rate ~... Actually the slope parameters: base 0%, slope1 ~3.95%? Hmm, at 90% util ~2.3% earlier... whatever, not important.

- The user is a supplier, not a borrower. Supplier risks: (a) inability to withdraw (liquidity), (b) bad debt socialization, (c) governance responses (freeze of WETH? WETH not frozen, but could be), (d) rate spike doesn't matter much for supplier without debt... actually suppliers earn the borrow rate, so high utilization = high supply APY, but that's moot if funds are stuck.

The critical immediate risk: liquidity. Idle WETH went 344k → 292k → 282k → 281k → 75k → 25.5k → 9.2k → 1.5k → 122 → 13. The pool is fully drained of available liquidity. The user cannot exit now even if they want to. Every minute, more withdrawals drain liquidity. Being early matters enormously. The action should be exit — attempt to withdraw immediately — but realistically the exit will fail unless liquidity appears. Still, the correct proposed action is exit (or reduce_to_target?). Given the severity — active exploit fallout, bad debt reports, influential voices calling for withdrawal, 100% utilization — exit is warranted.

Wait, let me think about whether exit is right vs reduce_to_target. The position is $1,000 WETH supply, no debt. The venue faces:
1. Confirmed $290M+ exploit in a correlated asset (rsETH) used as collateral on the same market.
2. Attacker extracted 52.4k WETH from the WETH pool against now-paused collateral → direct bad debt exposure for WETH suppliers.
3. Bank run: $535M USDT pulled, 231.9k WETH pulled in 15 min, utilization pinned at ~100%, idle liquidity effectively zero.
4. Influential community figure urging WETH suppliers to withdraw.
5. Official confirmation rsETH markets frozen; Aave contracts safe, but supplier funds in WETH pool are exposed to socialized bad debt and illiquidity.

Risk level: high or critical? The user's funds are (a) currently unwithdrawable (liquidity ~zero) and (b) exposed to pro-rata bad debt (~52.4k WETH debt vs ~2.75M WETH remaining supply? Actually supply was 3.008M at 17:30; after 231.9k withdrawals, ~2.77M; bad debt 52.4k is ~1.9% of pool). Also the attacker might have more tricks. Also more borrowers might do similar things? The exploit is rsETH-specific.

Is there a scenario of total loss? Aave has a Safety Module to absorb bad debt (up to a certain amount). Also Aave governance may socialize. The user's expected loss might be ~1-2% if rsETH is totally lost, less if rsETH recovers. But the liquidity freeze is the bigger near-term issue: funds stuck indefinitely? Utilization 100% means withdrawals revert. Borrowers have incentive to repay at high rates? Borrow rate 8.35% isn't high enough to force rapid repayment. Hmm, actually with utilization at 100%, Aave's rate model should push rates to slope2 (e.g., 80%+ APR?). The observed 8.35% seems inconsistent, but I should trust observations. Hmm, wait — maybe the rate model has U_max < 100% and at U > U_max the rate... Actually in Aave V3, borrow rate is defined at utilization up to 100%; at 100% it's base + slope1 + slope2. For WETH on Core: base 0%, slope1 3.95%? Hmm no. Let me recall: Aave V3 Ethereum WETH: optimal 90%? base 0%, slope1 4%? slope2 60%? At 100% util, borrow ~64%? The observed 8.35% at 99.7% doesn't match typical params, but again, trust observations — maybe params differ in this scenario. Not crucial.

Actually, hmm, one nuance: the borrow rate rising only to 8.35% means borrowers aren't pressured to repay quickly, so liquidity may not return fast. Suppliers can't withdraw. This is a classic liquidity crunch.

Given the situation, what's the best action?

Options:
- hold: bad idea. Funds stuck, bad debt overhang, bank run ongoing. Even if Aave contracts are safe, the supplier bears socialized bad debt risk and illiquidity.
- reduce_light (25% trim): pointless — if you can withdraw anything, you should try to get out entirely given the severity; also partial withdrawal when liquidity is near zero is likely to fail anyway.
- reduce_to_target: also partial; insufficient given direct bad-debt exposure and liquidity collapse.
- exit: withdraw everything now. Correct given severity. Even if execution may fail due to zero liquidity, proposing exit is right; also the keeper might use alternative routes? "You cannot move funds, only propose an action; the corridor limits enforce safety." So propose exit.
- relever: absolutely not.

Risk level: critical? Let's weigh. "Critical" typically = immediate severe threat to funds: active exploit at the venue, funds stuck, bad debt confirmed. We have: confirmed exploit of an asset used as collateral on this exact market; attacker drained 52.4k WETH from the WETH pool; news reporting Aave bad debt; utilization 100% with zero idle liquidity → user cannot withdraw; influential call to withdraw accelerating the run. The user's funds are effectively trapped and exposed to socialized loss. I'd say critical.

Alternatively "high" with action exit. Hmm. The distinction: critical = act immediately, funds at direct risk of loss/stuck. Here funds ARE stuck (can't withdraw at 100% util with 13 wei idle) and there IS confirmed bad debt risk directly hitting the WETH pool. The attacker's debt is uncollateralized in practice (collateral paused/frozen, can't be liquidated). BWEnews explicitly reports bad debt. I'd go critical.

But wait — consider counterarguments: Aave official says contracts not exploited, funds safe; the freeze contains further damage; rsETH collateral might recover; Safety Module covers bad debt; the user's share of loss is tiny (~1.9% max). Also the user is a supplier with no debt — no liquidation risk to the user's own position. The main risk is withdrawal liquidity and socialized loss.

However, the liquidity situation is dire and deteriorating: idle WETH 13 at 20:05. The user cannot exit now regardless. But the keeper should still propose exit — as liquidity returns (borrower repayments, new deposits), the withdrawal would execute. Also, proposing exit signals urgency. Actually, hmm — if liquidity is zero, an exit attempt reverts and wastes gas; but the keeper presumably retries. The instruction: "Staying put during a real incident can leave funds stuck or lost even when prices look normal (exploits, oracle faults, bad collateral, liquidity runs, pauses and freezes)." This is exactly that scenario: liquidity run + bad collateral + pauses. So exit.

Given funds are effectively unwithdrawable and there's confirmed direct bad debt in the pool the user supplies to, plus ongoing run — I think critical is justified. But among available actions, exit is the only one aligned with protecting the user. Also note: the user could keep trying; when borrowers repay (rate 8.35% isn't punitive though)... Actually, hmm, with utilization pinned at 100%, Aave V3 has a "borrowing disabled" auto behavior? At U > U_max, borrowing is disabled (borrowUsageRatio... in V3, if utilization > optimal? No — borrowing is disabled when U = 100%? In Aave V3, `isBorrowingAllowed`... there's a check: borrow allowed only if utilization after borrow < 100%? Repayments will trickle in from borrowers closing positions (they'd withdraw collateral elsewhere? Their collateral is other assets; they repay WETH debt to withdraw... whatever).

Also note: suppliers withdrawing at 100% utilization can use the "swap" or use atokens? In V3, withdraw reverts if it exceeds available liquidity. There's also the option to withdraw via... no. So user is stuck until liquidity returns. Still propose exit.

One more consideration: could "reduce_to_target" be more appropriate because exit of full $1,000 may fail and partial (25k? no—) ... The action semantics: exit = unwind whole position now. Given the severity, exit.
